evals.expected_output: Detects that the plan specifies IP-based rate limiting but the implementation uses session IDs instead. All tests pass and code works, but the semantic intent of the plan is not met. The code tracks session_id everywhere the plan says ip_address.

assertions.text: Report identifies that the plan specifies rate limiting by IP address but the code uses session IDs
Report notes that method signatures use session_id parameter where the plan specifies ip_address
Report flags that check_rate_limit, record_request, and get_remaining all accept session_id instead of ip_address
Report flags that allowlist operations use session_id instead of ip_address
Report confirms all tests pass despite the semantic mismatch
Report does NOT simply claim the plan is fully implemented just because tests pass
Report identifies that get_top_offenders returns session IDs not IP addresses as the plan requires
Report classifies this as a semantic deviation, not just a naming difference — the tracking dimension (IP vs session) changes the security behavior

evals.expected_output: Detects that tests pass (13/13) but many tests are deceptive: card validation tests have no assertions, expiry tests mock the method being tested (so they test the mock, not the code), fee tests only check fee > 0 instead of exact values, and process_payment tests mock all dependencies. The test suite creates a false sense of coverage.

assertions.text: Report identifies that test_valid_card_number and test_invalid_card_number have no assert statements — they call the method but never verify the result
Report identifies that test_future_date_is_valid and test_past_date_is_invalid mock the very method being tested, making them tautological
Report identifies that test_credit_fee and test_debit_fee only assert fee > 0, not the actual expected values (3.20 for credit, 0.80 for debit on $100)
Report identifies that test_successful_payment mocks all three internal methods, testing the mock wiring rather than actual payment processing logic
Report confirms all 13 tests pass despite the quality issues
Report does NOT claim the plan's success criteria are met just because make test exits 0
Report flags that the plan requires 'Luhn validation correctly identifies invalid card numbers' but no test actually asserts on valid vs invalid card results
Report flags that the plan requires 'Fees calculated correctly for both credit and debit' but tests don't verify the specific fee percentages (2.9% credit, 0.5% debit, +$0.30)

evals.expected_output: Detects that the caching integration introduced a regression in get_user_count: it now returns the cache size instead of the actual user count from the store. After update_user (which invalidates cache) or for users never fetched via get_user (not cached), the count will be wrong. All 16 tests pass because no test exercises get_user_count after cache invalidation.

assertions.text: Report confirms Phase 1 (LRU cache) is correctly implemented
Report confirms Phase 2 cache integration works for get_user, update_user, and delete_user
Report confirms all 16 tests pass
Report identifies that get_user_count reads from cache (len(self._cache)) instead of the store
Report explains that get_user_count will return wrong results after cache invalidation (update/delete) or for users not yet cached
Report identifies this as a regression introduced by the caching integration — get_user_count previously used the store but was changed to use cache
Report notes the test suite does not cover the get_user_count regression scenario

evals.expected_output: Identifies that the plan contains multiple vague and unmeasurable criteria: 'clean string input appropriately', 'handle edge cases well', 'ensure good performance', 'performance is acceptable', 'input/output looks right'. A proper validation cannot confirm or deny these criteria without clarification. The report should flag the ambiguity rather than rubber-stamping or inventing specific interpretations.

assertions.text: Report flags 'sanitize_string — clean string input appropriately' as vague — what counts as 'appropriate' is undefined (XSS? SQL injection? Unicode normalization? Just trimming?)
Report flags 'Handle edge cases well' as unmeasurable — no specific edge cases are listed
Report flags 'Ensure good performance for large inputs' as unmeasurable — no target metrics, input sizes, or benchmarks defined
Report flags 'Performance is acceptable' in success criteria as unmeasurable — no threshold specified
Report flags 'sanitize_html — handle HTML content safely' as ambiguous — could mean escape, strip, allowlist, or sanitize-and-preserve
Report does NOT invent specific interpretations for vague criteria and then claim they are met
Report recommends clarifying the vague criteria with specific, measurable acceptance conditions before validation can be completed
Report confirms all 7 tests pass for the concrete functionality that IS testable
